en: The *Sūtra on Filial Sons* Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin.
The Buddha asked the śramaṇas: “When parents give birth to a child, they carry it in their womb for ten months, bearing the burden of its body.”
Regarding illness:
on the day of birth, the mother is endangered and the father is terrified, a state of emotion difficult to describe.

Once born, [the parents] push aside their own dry bedding so the child may lie upon their dampness; through the height of their sincerity, their blood transforms into milk. They rub, wipe, bathe, clothe, feed, and instruct [the child]; they provide gifts and offerings to teachers and friends, and present tribute to rulers and elders.
If the child is harmonious and joyful, the parents are also delighted; if the child displays sorrow and distress, the parents' hearts wither away.
Their affection follows them as they leave the door, and they keep them in mind upon returning home; their hearts remain filled with apprehension, fearing that the child may do something unwholesome.
"The parental kindness is such as this; how can it be repaid?
The śramaṇas replied, "One should repay parental kindness only by offering service with utmost propriety and a compassionate heart."
The World-Honored One spoke again:

"Suppose a son nourishes his parents by providing every variety of ambrosial delicacy to satisfy their mouths, celestial music and manifold sounds to delight their ears, and famous garments and superior robes to adorn their bodies; and suppose he carries them on his shoulders, traveling throughout the four seas, exhausting his own life span to repay their kindness—can this be called filial piety?"
The śramaṇas said:
"Is there anything greater than this in the greatness of filial piety?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This is not yet filial piety!

If one's parents are obstinate and ignorant, failing to honor the Triple Gem; if they are cruel and violent, plundering and acting unreasonably; if they are lewd and lustful toward external objects; if they use false words contrary to the Way; if they are treacherous, arrogant, and chaotic, turning their backs on the upright and true—if they are as wicked as this, the child ought to offer the utmost remonstrance to awaken them."

If they remain dim-sighted and have not yet awakened, one should then employ transformation through meaning, drawing upon analogies and categories to show them the prisons of kings and the punishments and executions of prisoners, saying:
"These are those who followed deviant paths; their bodies were beset by manifold poisons, and they brought their own deaths upon themselves."
When life ends and the spirit departs, one is bound to Mount Tai; amidst the boiling water, fire, and myriad poisons, one cries out alone for rescue.
Because of the evil deeds committed there, one encounters such heavy calamity.

"Even if they have not yet moved on, they will wail and lament, weeping and crying out, refusing all food and drink; though their kin may not be wise, they will surely suffer the pain of their affection and fear that their son has died."

You should still exert yourself to restrain and subdue your mind, honoring the Way; if you can transform your intent to serve the Buddha and uphold the five precepts—being compassionate and refraining from killing, being pure and yielding and refraining from stealing, being chaste and refraining from lust, being trustworthy and refraining from deception, and being filial and obedient and refraining from intoxication—then within your own clan, parents will be kind and children filial, husbands will be upright and wives chaste, the nine branches of the family will live in harmony, and servants will be submissive. Your benevolence will spread far and wide, and all sentient beings who receive your favor will respond with gratitude. Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions, devas, dragons, ghosts, and spirits, as well as enlightened rulers and loyal, impartial ministers, and the myriad commoners, will all respect and love you, blessing and securing your peace.

If there are numerous instances of perverse governance, with favorites and concubines as ministers, and with wicked children and seductive women—ten thousand evils and myriad monsters—none of these can do anything to you.

Thus, your parents will dwell in peace throughout their lives; when they reach the end of their natural term, their spirits will be reborn in the heavens. There, they will join the assembly of all Buddhas to hear the words of the Dharma, attain the Way, transcend the world, and forever part from suffering.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"In this world, there is no filial piety greater than this; this alone is true filial piety.

To be able to cause one's parents to abandon evil and practice good, to uphold the five precepts, and to maintain the three refuges—dying in the evening after having honored them in the morning—is an act whose kindness exceeds that of a parent’s nursing and sustenance, and its bounty is immeasurable."
If one cannot transform one’s parents through the supreme transformation of the Three Honored Ones, then even if one provides filial support, it remains unfilial.

[Conversely,] if one fails to distance oneself from a wicked wife and does not remain close to the worthy—given that feminine emotions are full of desire, that one never tires of lust for beauty, and that such conduct violates filial piety and leads to the killing of one’s parents; and if state administration falls into chaos and the myriad people flee in exile;

whereas one’s original intent was to practice benevolent giving, to restrain oneself according to ritual propriety, to cultivate a gentle heart and honor benevolence, to fervently advance in virtue, to keep the mind hidden in stillness, and to pursue wisdom with a resolute will, such that one’s fame moved the heavens and one’s brilliance equaled the sages—yet instead, one defiles oneself by gathering around a wife, deludes the mind with female beauty, becomes dazed and lost in sensual desire, and displays a myriad variations of seductive and bewitching gestures.

Men of meager wisdom and shallow vision, beholding such things, fail to perceive their subtle gradations; they consequently turn their wills away from the truth and devote themselves to those malevolent spirits and demonic deceptions of perverse artifice. Some endanger their parents or kill their sovereign; they are stingy with wealth yet licentious in passion, resentful, envious, indolent, and arrogant. With distracted minds and blinded ignorance, their conduct becomes equal to that of birds and beasts. From time immemorial, there has never been one who did not, through such ways, bring about their own destruction and the extinction of their lineage.
Therefore, the śramaṇa remains solitary and does not pair; he purifies his will and makes the Way his primary concern.

By upholding these clear precepts, if he serves as a ruler, he shall protect the four seas; if he serves as a minister, he shall be loyal. He nourishes the people with benevolence, such that fathers emulate the clarity of the Dharma and sons practice filial piety and compassion; husbands are trustworthy and wives are chaste.
"When upāsakas and upāsikās practice in this manner, they shall encounter the Buddhas and behold the Dharma in every lifetime and attain the Way.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the disciples rejoiced.
The Sutra on Filial Sons Spoken by the Buddha
